claims.text: The baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy is equiatomic, with approximately 20 at.% of each element.
Prior studies provide known mechanical-performance data for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Systematic variation of elemental percentages can be correlated with microstructure and mechanical properties using a machine-learning model.
Combining targeted composition experiments with machine learning will reveal nonlinear, element-specific contributions to strength and ductility.
Controlling temperature, strain rate, annealing, and other processing variables can isolate the effects of composition changes.
Changing elemental fractions alters lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changing elemental fractions may produce local phase variations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changes in lattice distortion and local phase state mediate the influence of composition on mechanical behavior.
Changing individual elemental fractions alters the degree of solid-solution strengthening.
Composition-induced changes in solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion affect dislocation motion.
Changing individual elemental fractions affects phase stability.
A machine-learning model can capture nonlinear interdependencies among composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties across the sampled composition space.
The predictive model will identify compositional deviations that improve both strength and ductility relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Observed mechanical-property trends will follow the model's nonlinear predictions.
The proposed relationship is restricted to compositions that retain a single-phase random solid solution.
Compositions that undergo phase segregation or form intermetallic compounds are outside the stated applicability domain.
The model's predictive accuracy depends on the quality and compositional range of the experimental data.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator includes local phase variations, whereas the boundary limits the hypothesis to compositions maintaining a single-phase random solid solution. It is unclear whether the proposed phase variations are compatible with that boundary.
